slice: Triumph TF all models (setups, springs, feel, gearing) + Japanese off-road CRF-RX / KX-X / YZ-FX / WR setups and mods 2020-2026

records.statement: The 450-E's bottom end is strong but not violent; the midrange is its standout, and sixth gear gives a high top speed. Map 1 (light off) is the standard, more aggressive map; Map 2 (light on) is noticeably smoother and suits casual trail riding, while Map 1 suits racing.

source.name: Cycle News: 2026 Triumph TF 450-E Review

records.notes: Rider impressions on a launch ride in deep sand; no rpm figures given. E has no Wi-Fi module as standard, so custom maps need the optional module. Traction control not used; tester suggests it for slick or muddy conditions.

records.topic: E model final drive and gearbox
records.statement: The 450-E has a six-speed wide-ratio gearbox (the MX bikes have five close ratios) and 13/51 final drive against 13/48 on the 450 MX launch bike; the taller rear sprocket helps initial pull.

source.name: Cycle News: 2026 Triumph TF 450-E Review

records.notes: Sprocket counts as stated by the magazine; BAK holds the OEM manual ratios separately.

records.statement: On the Australian launch a tester set the 450-E to 108 mm race sag, preferred the stock race map (clean, torquey off the bottom, strong on top) and found the stock 13/51 gearing about right with well-spaced six-speed ratios.

source.name: ADB Magazine: Enduro launch 2026 Triumph TF 450-E

records.notes: Tester weight not stated. Spring rates are softer than the MX bikes but no figures given. Little engine braking and quiet at low revs reported.

records.topic: E model feel and map difference
records.statement: Testers found the 250-E strongest in the midrange and able to hold each gear longer, and the 450-E very manageable in the gentler map. The softer map gives a more gradual, energy-saving delivery for singletrack; the difference between maps is noticeable but not extreme.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E Review 2025

records.notes: Claimed figures as printed by the magazine; they differ from Triumph figures quoted elsewhere (e.g. 57.8 hp for the 450-E). The quickshifter sometimes refused a shift under hard acceleration.

records.statement: The E models' quickshifter is meant for clutchless upshifts under full load, but one test found it occasionally blocked the shift during hard acceleration.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E Review 2025

records.notes: Single tester report; called a minor complaint.

records.statement: On the Australian launch the 250-E was described as broad with a strong bottom end and the 450-E as linear with controllable torque. One tester preferred Map 1 (full power) on the 450-E, and traction control on a wet day worked well with little slip.

values.extra_maps: 6 via MX Tune app with optional Wi-Fi module (AUD 370)

source.name: Bike Review (AU): Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E enduro launch

records.notes: Australian-spec figures as quoted by the magazine.

records.topic: E model final drive (Australian launch spec)
records.statement: Australian launch spec lists 13/48 final drive for the 250-E and 13/51 for the 450-E.

source.name: Bike Review (AU): Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E enduro launch

records.notes: Conflicts with another test that says both E models run 13/51; the same article also lists the 250-E as five-speed while saying six-speed in its text, so treat as uncertain.

records.statement: A European test says both E models use a six-speed gearbox and 13/51 final drive, shorter than the MX models.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E Review 2025

records.notes: See conflicts: 250-E rear sprocket reported as 48 or 51.

records.statement: On a Canadian first ride a tester ran the TF 450-C at 108 mm race sag with stock clickers and the stock map; he switched traction control off because it made throttle response feel flat. The bike did not stall at low rpm in tight trails, unlike most 450s.

source.name: Motocross Performance Magazine: First Ride 2026 Triumph TF 450 C

records.notes: Described as a TF 450-X with softer suspension and an 18-inch rear tyre; quickshifter works on upshifts 2nd to 5th. No spring rates given. Compare: other testers ran 102 mm sag in tight woods.

records.statement: One test team's 2025 gearing guide runs the TF 250-X one tooth shorter than stock (13/49 instead of 13/48); the extra tooth helped third-gear recovery on an engine with a smooth roll-on.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested: 2025 MX Gearing Guide

records.notes: Motocross tracks (tight clay, sandy, East Coast loam). Stock engine or aftermarket muffler only.

records.topic: KX450X GP/desert race springs and valving
records.statement: A West Coast GP race build stiffened the 2023 KX450X one step at each end (fork 0.49 to 0.50 kg/mm, shock 5.3 to 5.4 kg/mm) with stiffer valving, run at 103-105 mm race sag with an aftermarket linkage arm, to hold up in big braking bumps and whoops.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: Tuned 2023 Kawasaki KX450X project bike build

records.notes: Rider weights not given (big and small high-level testers). Valving by a suspension shop, no shim detail. Linkage arm said to improve traction on acceleration bumps.

records.statement: For the 2023 KX450X one test team chose 13/50 as the best all-round GP gearing, 13/47 for open desert (more top speed while still pulling technical bits) and 13/51 or 13/52 for mountain riding for more low-end grunt.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: Tuned 2023 Kawasaki KX450X project bike build

records.notes: 13/50 described as one tooth smaller in the rear than stock X gearing.

records.statement: On the 2023 KX450X, a stock-ECU reflash smoothed the first crack of throttle and made power more progressive and broader; an aftermarket exhaust had a similar smoothing and broadening effect, and the two together were called a fast combination.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: Tuned 2023 Kawasaki KX450X project bike build

records.notes: No dyno numbers published. 2021-2023 engine generation.

records.statement: A 10 oz (about 283 g) bolt-on flywheel weight on a 2023 KX450X made revs build more slowly, the bike feel more planted and easier to accelerate without breaking traction, and less likely to stall, while still hitting hard; testers called the change subtle.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: Steahly flywheel weight for KX450X

records.notes: Tested off-road and on track; about 20 minutes to install. No rpm-specific data.

records.statement: Yamaha's 50 g (1.8 oz) flywheel weight adds about 15% flywheel inertia to the YZ450FX. Testers felt throttle jolts smooth out off idle and at low speed and less stall risk in tight terrain, but revs build more slowly, so with 14/52 gearing faster riders found third gear harder to pull out of corners.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: GYTR flywheel weight for YZ450FX

records.notes: Tested on a 2026 YZ450FX; part listed for YZ450F/FX. Needs a 24 mm internally threaded flywheel puller. Less suited to fast riders in sand.

records.statement: The 2025 KX250X engine puts more emphasis on low and midrange torque than the previous high-revving generation, which made technical off-road riding easier.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: First Impression 2025 Kawasaki KX250X

records.notes: Hare and hound terrain and woods loop; no rpm figures.

records.statement: The 2025 KX250X Showa suspension is lighter sprung and valved than the KX250 MX bike: supple in the woods, but on a fast grass track the fork dove deep on braking and felt harsh, fixed by adding a few clicks of fork compression and speeding rebound one click, at 105 mm race sag. Stock first gear is tall for technical terrain.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: First Impression 2025 Kawasaki KX250X

records.notes: Exact click counts and tester weight not given.

records.statement: The 2023 KX250X pulls from just above idle to over 12,000 rpm with a progressive build and flat torque curve, but it needs revs to lift the front wheel and can stall pulling away cold with no throttle. Testers used the Soft coupler throughout; first gear was raised, which meant more clutch slipping on technical trails.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling: 2023 Kawasaki KX250X review

records.notes: Three couplers (Standard, Hard, Soft); custom maps need the KX FI Calibration Kit (quoted $775). Suspension plush; fork bottomed only on brutal downhills.

records.statement: For desert hare and hound racing, one build on a 2024 KX250X fitted the 2023 KX450X's Showa suspension and ran about 106 mm sag with the fork flush and axle further back. Gearing went from stock 13/50 to 14/48 (too tall, hard on the clutch in rocks) and settled on 14/50; an ECU remap improved power everywhere but low-end torque was still lacking.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2024 Kawasaki KX250X off-road build stage 1

records.notes: Swapped suspension never used the last 2-3 inches of travel and struggled in slow rocks. 80-mile hare and hound plus 40-mile technical loop.

records.statement: The 2025 KX450X has good low-rpm torque without a hard hit, builds through the midrange and keeps pulling into the top end, which testers likened to a 350. App Map 2 is about 10-15% tamer than Map 1.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2025 Kawasaki KX450X test

records.notes: Compared with the previous-generation engine's harder low-rpm hit.

records.statement: On the 2025 KX450X, power mode and traction control changes need the engine idling and the button held for close to three seconds, so they are not on-the-fly. Traction control level 1 trims throttle response slightly; level 2 is quite noticeable.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2025 Kawasaki KX450X test

records.notes: A stock-ECU remap by an aftermarket tuner gave large gains (no numbers published).

records.statement: Stock KX450X suspension is soft for West Coast off-road: the fork rides low and pitches on braking for fast or heavy riders, and the shock wallows and bottoms softly in big braking bumps and whoops. Testers ran 105-108 mm sag, fork flush in the clamps, and a shorter shock shaft or lowering link so less preload gives the same ride height.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2025 Kawasaki KX450X test

records.notes: Applies to stock and revalved suspension. Tester weights not given.

records.statement: With a 13-tooth front, one test team runs the 2025 KX450X at 13/47-13/48 for desert, 13/50 for GP and motocross (best all-round), and 13/51-13/52 for mountains and trees. Stock first gear is sometimes too tall for tight terrain and fifth too short for desert.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2025 Kawasaki KX450X test

records.notes: Same team's 2023 choices were 13/47, 13/50 and 13/51-52.

records.topic: KX450X clutch plate failure in sand racing
records.statement: One test KX450X broke a clutch plate at 27 hours after several hard sand races; the testers recommend replacing plates and fibres every 10-20 hours under racing, changing oil every 5-6 hours, and suggest aftermarket plates.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2025 Kawasaki KX450X test

records.notes: Single test bike under abusive 2-hour sand races; Kawasaki recommends non-synthetic oil.

records.statement: The 2024 KX450X has a noticeably softer bottom end and revs longer on top like a 250F; stock it handles quickly but lacks a little high-speed stability and the front twitches under hard braking, so the tester stiffened the fork and added a couple of rebound clicks to hold it higher. An app map built with more low-end response kept the top-end revs.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2024 Kawasaki KX450X full review

records.notes: Map values not published. Bike runs hot in tight technical trails.

records.topic: YZ450FX desert/GP build springs and gearing
records.statement: A desert and GP race build on a 2022 YZ450FX fitted stiffer 0.48-0.50 kg/mm fork springs and a stiffer shock spring with minor valving changes for better bump absorption and bottoming resistance, and changed gearing from 13/50 to 14/52, which settled the chassis under acceleration and made second gear usable in corners.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: Tuned 2022 Yamaha YZ450FX bike build phase 1

records.notes: Shock rate not given. A plug-in WR450F stator (~100 W) was fitted to power lights; the FX stator has little spare output.

records.statement: A 200 lb tester in tight, muddy South Carolina woods ran the 2024 YZ450FX at 104 mm sag, used the mellow map further detuned in the app with traction control added, and slowed fork rebound to calm a soft, sometimes harsh fork; he felt the stock springs were slightly light for his weight.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX off-road racer first impression

records.notes: Compared with the YZ450F, first gear is very low, second slightly lower and fifth taller. Suspension internally lowered (10 mm less stroke).

records.statement: On a 2026 YZ450FX in Southern California high desert, the stock engine felt aggressive, and a tuned app map gave smooth, broad delivery with easier throttle control; the KYB suspension felt stiff and race-oriented and the tester slowed rebound for a more planted feel. Fork and shock compression clickers can be adjusted by hand.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: First Impression 2026 Yamaha YZ450FX

records.notes: Map values, sag and tester weight not given.

records.statement: The 2023 CRF450RX pulls strongly and controllably from low to mid with a more linear delivery than before, is slightly short on top end, and its light flywheel makes it prone to stalling as speed drops.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2023 Honda CRF450RX review

records.notes: Maps make a clear difference but are hard to change on the fly.

records.statement: On the 2023 CRF450RX, stock fork height (5 mm up) caused oversteer, so testers ran the fork flush, 105-108 mm sag, and a shock shaft a couple of mm shorter (or longer link arm) to cure a rear-high feel. Gearing went from 13/50 to 14/52 for a smoother curve, better over-rev and fewer shifts; the five-speed still runs out of gear early.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2023 Honda CRF450RX review

records.notes: Suspension among the stiffest stock 450 off-road bikes; small clicker changes have large effects. Testers suggest stiffer springs to hold it higher but give no rates.

records.statement: The 2025 CRF450RX still hits like a motocross bike low in the revs even in its softest map; around 12 mph first gear is too abrupt and second can feel close to stalling, so it is best in open terrain. The CRF250RX has more low-end than other 250s and its off-road map smooths the step into the stronger part of the curve, suiting tight trails.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: Riding the 2025 Honda CRF450RX and CRF250RX, the wrap

records.notes: Tested on tight trials-facility trails kept mostly under 24 mph.

records.statement: Starting from Honda's CRF250RX settings (fork compression 10, rebound 14, 5 mm up; shock high-speed 2 1/3 turns, low-speed 10, rebound 15, 105 mm sag), one tester ended on fork compression 11 and rebound 13 out, shock high-speed 2 2/3 turns out, and 104 mm sag after about 6 hours.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested: 2025 Honda CRF250RX weekend warrior review

records.notes: Bike arrived at 6 mm fork height and 102 mm sag. Suspension felt tuned more for GNCC than aggressive MX. Tester weight not stated.

records.statement: On the 2025 CRF250RX, Map 1 (stock) is like Map 3 but softer everywhere with less over-rev and suited fast singletrack; Map 2 is a linear, easy roll-on for tight, slow trails or newer riders; Map 3 is aggressive and revs quickly with good over-rev, though it could use more punch out of corners.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested: 2025 Honda CRF250RX weekend warrior review

records.notes: Map 3 used on track.

records.statement: Lowering the 2025 CRF250RX triple-clamp pinch bolts from 16/15 lb-ft to 12/10 lb-ft cut the rigidity felt in the hands, softened flat landings and improved front-wheel compliance.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested: 2025 Honda CRF250RX weekend warrior review

records.notes: Tester modification below the manual spec; use at own risk. Engine mount bolts also reduced, values not published.

records.statement: A desert and GP revalve on a 2020 YZ250FX used stiffer springs front and rear, plusher initial valving with more hold-up, and fork oil raised from 295 cc stock to about 320 cc and then 365 cc, giving less wallow, better bottoming resistance and more hold in corners.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: suspension revalve for 2020 YZ250FX (product test)

records.notes: Spring rates and rider weight not published. Lake Havasu GP and WORCS racing.

records.statement: One Australian setup guide recommends a 95-100 mm race sag on the 2025 WR250F, smaller than usual, to balance the chassis; the stock fork works for average riders but feels harsh through the arms over chop for faster riders.

source.name: Transmoto: 2025 WR250F suspension set-up tips

records.notes: Remaining settings are in the source's video and were not extracted.

records.topic: 2025 WR250F stock setup for a 90 kg rider
records.statement: A 90 kg tester rode the 2025 WR250F on grass track, enduro loop and trails without changing compression, rebound or sag and rated the KYB suspension a standout; he found the six-speed gearing right from tight singletrack to fire roads, the engine smooth to a high rev limit, and it was a little easy to stall at first.

source.name: AMCN: Dirt test 2025 Yamaha WR250F

records.notes: Australian model.

records.statement: In steep, rocky Idaho singletrack the 2025 WR250F's KYB suspension was firm and precise at speed but a bit stiff for slow technical trails; the hand-adjustable fork compression knob was used for trailside tweaks.

source.name: Upshift: 2025 Yamaha WR250F tested in Idaho's high country

records.notes: No settings published; date inferred from the page.
